2.1.1.1.reason: This control requires senior leadership to mandate and oversee a cloud security program and allocate budget, personnel, and technology resources. These are organisational governance and management decisions; Azure resource properties, identity settings, and platform signals cannot establish that leadership direction or adequate resourcing has occurred, so Azure Policy cannot assert compliance.
2.1.1.1.evidence_source: Board or executive-approved cloud security program charter, governance committee terms of reference and meeting minutes, assigned roles and responsibilities, and approved budget and resource-allocation records.

2.1.1.2.reason: This control requires the cloud consumer to establish and document cloud security governance policies and maintain a process for identifying and complying with applicable legal and regulatory obligations. These are organisational, legal and governance activities; Azure Policy may support implementation of selected technical requirements, but it cannot determine whether the governance framework is complete, approved, or legally adequate.
2.1.1.2.evidence_source: Approved cloud security governance framework and policies; legal and regulatory obligations register; compliance assessment records; policy approval and review minutes; assigned ownership and periodic compliance review evidence.

2.1.2.1.reason: The control primarily requires the organisation to establish and operate a continuous risk management programme covering cloud services, including lifecycle risk assessment, monitoring, treatment, and mitigation. Azure security findings may inform that programme, but no Azure resource property or tenant setting can demonstrate that the programme is robust, approved, continuously performed, or that identified risks are appropriately assessed and treated.
2.1.2.1.evidence_source: Approved cloud risk management framework and procedures; cloud risk register with owners, treatment plans, acceptance decisions, and review history; periodic risk assessment reports and governance meeting minutes.

2.1.2.2.reason: Microsoft Purview classification and sensitivity labels can provide Azure evidence that data classification is applied, while Azure security configurations can demonstrate selected protection measures aligned to those classifications. However, Azure Policy cannot determine whether a security and privacy risk assessment was conducted or whether its impact analysis is appropriate; those elements require documented human governance and review.
2.1.2.2.evidence_source: Microsoft Purview Data Map and sensitivity-label reports; approved cloud security and privacy risk assessments, data classification register, risk treatment plans, and review/approval records.

2.1.2.3.reason: This control requires stakeholder communication and consultation throughout risk assessments, followed by senior leadership’s documented acknowledgement and formal acceptance of cloud migration risks. These are governance decisions and human approval activities; Azure Policy cannot determine whether executives understood, discussed, and accepted identified risks before data and operations were moved to the cloud.
2.1.2.3.evidence_source: Approved cloud risk assessments and risk register, stakeholder consultation and communication records, executive meeting minutes, and signed risk acceptance or cloud migration approval records.

2.1.3.1.evidence_source: Approved personnel-security policy mapped to the UAE Information Assurance Standard; employee, vendor, and contractor screening and onboarding records; confidentiality and security clauses; training acknowledgements; access termination checklists; and periodic compliance review records maintained in the GRC/HR system.

2.1.3.2.reason: The control requires the cloud consumer to establish contractual clauses covering CSP personnel screening, roles and segregation of duties, awareness training, disciplinary measures, and orderly termination. These are contractual and governance obligations rather than Azure resource or identity configurations, so no Azure Policy can determine whether the required clauses exist or are adequate.
2.1.3.2.evidence_source: Executed Microsoft cloud services agreement and applicable contractual addenda, documented shared-responsibility/RACI matrix, supplier due-diligence records, and contract review and termination procedures maintained in the customer’s GRC repository.

2.1.4.1.reason: The control requires the cloud consumer to understand and document what information Microsoft’s subprocessors and supply-chain parties may receive or access. Azure resource properties cannot demonstrate that organisational awareness; compliance depends on supplier due diligence, review of Microsoft contractual disclosures and subprocessors, and ongoing governance of information-sharing risks.
2.1.4.1.evidence_source: Third-party and supply-chain risk assessment; approved supplier due-diligence records; information/data-flow inventory; Microsoft Data Protection Addendum and Online Services Subprocessor List review records.

2.1.4.2.reason: This control requires the cloud consumer to identify and assess security risks arising from third-party and supply-chain resources. 2.1.4.2.evidence_source: Approved third-party and supply-chain risk management procedure; supplier inventory; completed supplier security risk assessments; supply-chain risk register; and associated review or approval records.

2.1.4.3.reason: This control requires the cloud consumer to liaise with Microsoft and assess whether third-party suppliers meet applicable cloud security requirements. 2.1.4.3.evidence_source: Third-party risk management procedure, CSP and supplier due-diligence records, Microsoft compliance documentation reviewed from the Service Trust Portal, correspondence with Microsoft, supplier assessment reports, and review or approval minutes.

2.1.5.2.evidence_source: Microsoft Service Trust Portal documentation, including Azure SOC 2 Type II reports, ISO/IEC 27001 certification and independent audit reports, supplemented by the customer’s documented review and acceptance of those reports.

2.2.2.2.reason: This control requires the cloud consumer to negotiate, approve, and retain contractual terms covering portability, termination and data retrieval, and dispute resolution under UAE governing law. 2.2.2.2.evidence_source: Executed cloud service agreement and SLA, including portability and exit clauses, termination and data-retrieval procedures, UAE governing-law and dispute-resolution clauses, supported by legal review and contract approval records.

2.3.2.2.reason: Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM configuration can evidence that cryptographic keys are maintained in a designated managed key store, while Azure RBAC role assignments and Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management can demonstrate separation between key-management and key-usage duties. 2.3.2.2.evidence_source: Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM inventory and configuration; Azure RBAC role assignments and access review records; Entra PIM activation and audit logs; documented key management standard and trusted-provider assessment.

2.3.2.3.evidence_source: Approved cryptographic risk assessment documenting the HYOK analysis, decision rationale, risk acceptance or treatment, responsible approvers, and review records.

2.3.2.4.evidence_source: Approved risk assessment identifying the need for HYOK; Microsoft Purview Double Key Encryption configuration; external customer-controlled key service or HSM configuration, access-control records, and key usage/audit logs.

2.3.2.5.reason: The control requires the customer to implement a hold-your-own-key architecture in which key access, revocation, and audit remain available independently of Microsoft as the cloud service provider. 2.3.2.5.evidence_source: Microsoft Purview Information Protection/Azure Rights Management configuration exports showing HYOK protection settings, supplemented by customer-operated AD RMS or HSM access-control configuration, key-revocation test records, and external key audit logs.
